questions.question: BEM stands for:
questions.explanation: BEM is a naming methodology: Block (component), Element (part of block, __), Modifier (variant, --).

questions.question: The BEM class for a 'button' inside a 'card' block, in a 'primary' variant:
questions.explanation: block__element--modifier: card (block) + __button (element) + --primary (modifier). Single class per node, flat specificity.

questions.question: A key benefit of BEM is:

options.text: Flat, predictable specificity (single-class selectors) and self-documenting structure

questions.explanation: BEM uses one class per element, so specificity stays (0,0,1,0) — avoids specificity wars and makes styles portable.

questions.question: In BEM, an Element is denoted by:
questions.explanation: Elements use block__element. Modifiers use --, blocks stand alone. This keeps the three-part convention clear.

questions.question: A Modifier represents:

options.text: A state or variant of a block/element (e.g. disabled, large, theme)

questions.explanation: Modifiers (--primary, --disabled) flag variations without creating new blocks — keep base styles and extend.

questions.question: Why avoid nesting BEM elements like block__el1__el2?

options.text: It breaks the block/element model; elements belong to the block, not other elements

questions.explanation: BEM elements are flat: block__child, not block__parent__child. Deep nesting couples styles to structure.

questions.question: BEM helps avoid specificity issues because it encourages:
questions.explanation: Each node gets one class → specificity is always (0,0,1,0). Predictable overrides without escalating selectors.

questions.question: In a component framework (Angular), BEM pairs well because:

options.text: Component-scoped templates map cleanly to blocks, keeping styles readable and conflict-free

questions.explanation: BEM's block = component mental model; combined with framework view encapsulation, styles stay modular and clear.
